title: Why our merges wait in line on a free GitHub account

params.title: Why our merges wait in line

spoken.said: This is an open question, not an explainer. Two repositories, one person, and a crowd of agent sessions all merge into GitHub on a free personal account, and the merges wait in line. I'll show where the time goes, with the numbers, what we settled on, and why we still don't like it. If you know a better pattern that stays on GitHub and costs nothing, that's the part I'm asking for. It's as of November twenty-first, twenty twenty-six.

params.title: The filter matched four JSON files as Rust

spoken.narration: The job that decides what runs logged why. A filter called rust matched every one of the four files. Logged out, GitHub shows this log only to people signed in, so these lines are copied from it, word for word.

params.title: A negation, read as one more way to match

spoken.narration: Here is the cause. Each list ends with a pattern meant to leave Markdown out. But the filter's default rule is that a file counts when any one pattern matches it, and 'not Markdown' matches nearly every file there is. So the Rust flag and the Node flag were on for almost every pull request.

params.title: What a better pattern has to keep

rows.note: the code, the runs and the reviews stay there
no paid plan, no runner minutes bought
main is never red from two green branches
it is what makes drift loud

spoken.narration: So the answer has to keep four things. It stays on GitHub. It costs nothing. Main never goes red because two green branches met for the first time after merging. And CI stays, because it is what makes drift loud, even on the days it finds nothing.

params.title: Settle every branch, then land them together

steps.label: Settle
steps.note: Review, fixes and local checks, before any PR

steps.label: Bucket
steps.note: Three to five settled branches in one PR

steps.label: One CI round
steps.note: Instead of one per branch, per merge

steps.label: Fix the filter
steps.note: CI1, with two gates, in flight

spoken.narration: What we settled on has two parts. First, a branch does all its settling before it ever opens a pull request: review, fixes, and the checks a laptop can run. Then three to five settled branches land together in one bucket, so one CI round covers all of them. Second, fix the filter, so a change only runs the jobs it can fail.

rows.note: one flaky test holds back every branch in it

rows.command: pick it out of a bucket
rows.note: is coarser: it lands with its bucket
a ledger or fixture lands here first, then the server re-runs
both repos share the runners; the queue never clears

spoken.narration: Buckets trade one pain for others. A single flaky test now holds back several branches, not one. Reverting a feature means picking it back out of a bucket. Changes that come in pairs across the two repositories still go one after the other. And both repositories share one pool of runners, so under load the queue never clears.

params.title: Is there a better pattern, free, on GitHub?

rows.note: move the repos to a free organization: the queue is offered there
a bot branch that tests a batch once, then fast-forwards main
loose gate on the PR, full suite on main, revert on red
the one we haven't thought of

spoken.narration: Here's where I'd like help. A free organization seems to get the merge queue on public repositories, so moving there might be the whole answer, if nothing else breaks. Or a train: a bot branch that tests a batch once and then fast-forwards main. Or a looser gate on the pull request, the full suite on main, and a revert when it goes red. Each one gives something up. Which would you pick, or what are we missing?

spoken.said: The audit's data and scripts, and the workflow file, are public in the some-ui repository, and the description links each. If you have a pattern that keeps all four constraints, the issue is open.
